abstract: |
  Can graph neural predictions improve mixed-integer optimization when preparation costs and censoring are considered? We study capacitated facility location with class-aware partial starts: predictions of value 1 receive priority over abundant zeros, and Gurobi completes unspecified variables without restricting the feasible region. A bipartite predictor uses 54 quality-screened parents with fixed training, validation and test partitions. We distinguish historical six-medium evidence from a retrospective comparison on ten previously exposed test parents. Of 210 preserved records, the principal analysis uses 150 seed-42 observations across three methods and five CPU caps: 97 solver-reported terminal-target attainments and 53 censored observations. Attainments are not exact certificates; two medium parents retain numerical restrictions. The root-LP comparator matches the learned start's support budget and positive count and is not an independent LP heuristic. We separate neural speedup, CPU scaling, terminal quality and preparation-cost scenarios. A matched-work seed-42 training pair compares one-GPU serial training with four-GPU distributed training over 100 epochs and 3,400 updates. Distributed training accelerates the training loop by 2.167 times and the whole job by 1.831 times, but increases assigned GPU-hours and reduces selected parent-macro F1 from 0.7231 to 0.6906, exceeding the predeclared descriptive loss margin. These heterogeneous speed-quality-cost tradeoffs do not establish uniform superiority or preserved predictive quality. An authorized longer-horizon CPU campaign is in progress; its final results remain pending.

# Introduction

Capacitated facility location combines discrete facility decisions with capacity-constrained allocation. Mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) preserves a general mathematical framework for these decisions, but difficult instances can retain substantial primal-dual gaps after hours of computation. Learning assignment patterns from related instances offers a possible source of guidance. Its value depends on helping the solver, beyond predicting labels accurately.

We use MILPBench CFL instances [@milpbench]. A graph neural network (GNN) represents variable-constraint relationships and supplies selected binary values to Gurobi as a partial start. Unspecified variables remain for the solver to complete, with constraints and domains unchanged.

The research question is: under what conditions do predicted starts benefit or harm fixed-budget CFL optimization, including preparation cost? Class-aware selection prioritizes scarce predicted ones over abundant zeros. We compare BASE (B), without an external start; RELAX (R), using root-relaxation values; and GNN-START (G), using a frozen predictor. R matches G's assignment and one-count budgets and is not an independent LP-only heuristic. Historically exposed tests support retrospective evaluation, not independent generalization.

The contribution connects graph-based assignment prediction to native partial starts and assesses predictive quality separately from solver outcomes. @fig-pipeline summarizes the offline learning and online guidance stages.

![Offline learning and online solver guidance.](figures/figure_pipeline.pdf){#fig-pipeline width=100%}

The upper row prepares labels, graphs and the model; validation selects the checkpoint and policy. The lower row applies the frozen predictor to a label-free graph and supplies a partial start to a fresh solve. What transfers is the model and policy, not the new instance's solution.

# Related work

## Learning to Optimize

Learning to Optimize (L2O) learns useful solver decisions rather than necessarily replacing optimization [@bengio2021; @chen2022primer]. Within the acceleration, estimation and adaptation perspectives of @chen2024tutorial, our network proposes values that a solver checks and completes.

Learned information can supply constraints [@qu2026], starting scenarios [@goerigk2025] or nonlinear solution-generation mechanisms [@tang2024l2o]. Our native binary Start values leave the feasible region unchanged.

## Graph representations and solver decisions

Our architectural foundation is the variable-constraint bipartite network of @gasse2019, adapted from branching to binary-start prediction. Graph-based combinatorial reasoning [@cappart2021] also supports search-node comparison [@labassi2022], objective prediction [@scavuzzo2024] and cut selection [@zhang2026]; these have different targets and solver interfaces.

GCN uses degree-normalized propagation [@kipf2017], GraphSAGE separates centre and neighbourhood aggregation [@hamilton2017], and GAT/GATv2 learn neighbour weights [@velickovic2018; @brody2022]. Our coefficient-aware bipartite model uses neither of those attention operators. In opinion-dynamics regression, @vargas2025 compare architectures with explicit validation-selected settings; their rankings do not establish a preferred architecture for CFL. Expressiveness results for branching [@chen2024branching] and quadratic programs [@chen2024quadratic] likewise concern specific tasks.

## Primal guidance

MIP-GNN already includes neural warm-starting [@khalil2022]; we claim neither the first GNN--MIP integration nor representation novelty. Neural Diving completes partial assignments through sub-MIPs [@nair2020], whereas Predict-and-Search uses prediction-centred trust regions [@han2023].

Uncertainty-based reduction solves iteratively restricted subproblems [@canturk2024]; prediction-guided neighbourhoods [@ding2020] and local branching [@fischetti2003] likewise differ from native unrestricted `Start` completion [@gurobi2026]. Our rule prioritizes scarce ones under bounded support, without proving causal selector superiority. Situated among learned branch-and-bound components [@scavuzzo2026survey], the contribution is controlled CFL evaluation of heterogeneous effects and costs.

# Proposed method

## Instances and labels

Let $p$ identify an original benchmark instance, referred to as a parent when tracking data lineage. Its mathematical program is

$$
\begin{aligned}
z_p^\star &= \min_x\; c_p^\top x+c_{p,0},\\
A_p x &\mathrel{\bowtie_p} b_p,\\
\ell_p\leq x &\leq u_p,\qquad x_j\in\mathbb Z\quad(j\in I_p).
\end{aligned}
$$

Here, $A_p$ and $b_p$ define the linear constraints, $c_p$ and $c_{p,0}$ the objective, and $I_p$ the integer variables. The symbol $\bowtie_p$ denotes each row's inequality or equality sense. The original identities, coefficients, bounds, row senses, and objective constant are preserved. All experiments explicitly set the objective sense to MINIMIZE, overriding the MAXIMIZE headers in the supplied files. Input hashes and both objective senses are recorded, so that this study's minimization convention can be reproduced. Variable predictions are aligned with the original column identities rather than an assumed naming convention.

Let $B_p\subseteq I_p$ contain the binary variables. A feasible incumbent, meaning the best feasible solution retained by the solver, supplies target values $y_{pj}\in\{0,1\}$. Before admitting a label, we check variable coverage, bounds, integrality, every linear constraint, and reconstruction of the objective value. We also require a finite terminal relative MIP gap no greater than 0.10. Thus, admitted labels are feasible solutions within the specified quality threshold; they may be approximate rather than optimal.

## Instance classes and descriptive characterization

MILPBench groups the 90 original CFL instances into 30 easy, 30 medium, and 30 hard instances. These are benchmark difficulty categories, distinct from the binary target classes used in class-aware prediction. Our learning cohort contains all 30 easy instances and the 24 medium instances whose labels satisfy the admission threshold. The optimization experiments retain the original instance identities and evaluate medium instances separately from the pooled predictive assessment.

## Offline graph learning

Variables and constraints form nodes connected by nonzero coefficients in $A_p$. Each edge carries its coefficient. Variable features encode objective, bounds, type and root-LP value captured at the first optimal root-node MIPNODE callback; constraint features encode right-hand side and sense. Root values are aligned by variable identity. Reference labels read by the graph encoder support its separate feasibility audit; they do not enter the neural forward or start selection.

The seven variable channels are transformed objective coefficient, lower bound, upper bound, three type indicators, and root value. The five row channels are transformed right-hand side, three sense indicators, and a constant. A single edge channel encodes the coefficient. Numerical coefficients and bounds use signed $\log(1+|t|)$ after clipping to $[-60000,60000]$; infinite bounds use the corresponding endpoint. Root values are clipped without logarithmic scaling. These numerical encodings affect learning inputs, not the original solver model; clipping counts are audited.

The Gasse-inspired network predicts binary values rather than strong-branching choices. It uses two width-32 cycles, whereas the upstream baseline has one width-64 cycle. Two cycles extend local information exchange; a modest width limits the capacity and cost of the message functions. These considerations motivate a parsimonious fixed model, but no recorded architecture search establishes that 2×32 is preferable. Our concatenated message inputs also differ from the upstream additive feature transforms. For cycle $t$, row and variable embeddings update as

$$
\begin{aligned}
c_i^t&=\operatorname{ReLU}f_C^t\!\left(c_i^{t-1}\Vert P_C^t\!\sum_{j\in N(i)}g_C^t(c_i^{t-1}\Vert v_j^{t-1}\Vert e_{ij})\right),\\
v_j^t&=\operatorname{ReLU}f_V^t\!\left(v_j^{t-1}\Vert P_V^t\!\sum_{i\in N(j)}g_V^t(c_i^t\Vert v_j^{t-1}\Vert e_{ij})\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $N$ denotes neighbours, $\Vert$ concatenation, $e_{ij}$ the encoded coefficient, and $f/g$ two-layer perceptrons. Fixed affine prenorms $P$ use training graphs only; the variable update uses fresh row embeddings. A final perceptron gives binary-variable logits $s_{pj}$ and scores $q_{pj}=\sigma(s_{pj})$. Training minimizes positive-class-weighted binary cross-entropy (BCE),

$$\ell_{pj}=-w_+y_{pj}\log\sigma(s_{pj})-(1-y_{pj})\log(1-\sigma(s_{pj})),$$

where $w_+$ is the training negative-to-positive target ratio. This increases the rare positive class's loss contribution. Weighted-BCE scores are not automatically calibrated probabilities [@gneiting2007], and validation-F1 thresholding is not probability calibration.

Adam uses learning rate $10^{-3}$, a conventional default supported by @kingma2015. Gradient-norm clipping at 1 limits large gradients; @pascanu2013 motivate the stabilization principle, without validating this numerical threshold for CFL. The 100-epoch ceiling bounds training, and parent-balanced sampling gives each training parent four draws per epoch. Validation weighted BCE selects the checkpoint; validation F1 selects $\tau=0.9991843104362488$. The historical CPU model uses graph batches of one; the later matched GPU experiment uses global batch four to equalize work per update. These settings define the evaluated model; their sensitivity is unmeasured. Evaluation metrics are defined in @sec-metrics.

## Class-aware partial starts

For $q_j=\sigma(s_j)$, let $\hat y_j=\mathbf1[q_j\geq\tau]$. With $n=|B_p|$, define

$$K=\min\{n,20000,\max(1,\lfloor0.10n\rfloor)\}.$$

The support of a partial start is the set of variables for which values are supplied; $K$ is its maximum size. Selection first takes up to $K$ predicted ones in decreasing $q_j$ order, then fills any remaining places with predicted zeros in decreasing $1-q_j$ order. Variable names resolve ties consistently. This is the class-aware step: positive and negative predictions are ranked separately, giving priority to the scarce predicted ones. If no score reaches the positive threshold, the policy abstains. The 10% support fraction and 20,000-variable cap limit the amount of supplied information.

Selected values are assigned to Gurobi's `Start` attribute, while other values remain undefined. Gurobi then attempts to complete or repair this partial candidate as part of its solution process. We verify that the objective, matrix, row senses, and bounds have identical mathematical signatures before and after submission.

For comparison, the root-LP start uses the relaxation rather than the network to select variables. Suppose the GNN supplies $K'$ values, including $r$ ones. The comparator assigns 1 to the $r$ binary variables with the largest relaxation values and 0 to the $K'-r$ remaining variables with the smallest relaxation values. Root values are clipped to $[0,1]$ before ranking; variable names break ties. R and G therefore match assignment and one counts, while their selected indices may differ. Their preparation dependencies are included in cost accounting.

# Experimental design

The following single-thread, six-medium-instance design documents the historical
study preserved in the publication archive. The separate MVP2 seed42 analysis
and its exposed population are specified in @sec-mvp2-current; the historical
tables are not a replacement for that principal analysis.

## Populations and information boundaries

The learning cohort contains 54 quality-screened original instances: 30 easy and 24 medium. It is divided into 34 training, ten validation, and ten predictive-test parents. @tbl-populations identifies the purpose of each partition and distinguishes predictive testing from the separate optimization comparison.

| Stage | Parents | Permitted information | Purpose |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Fitting | 34 training originals | Admitted labels and graphs | Gradient updates and prenorm |
| Predictor selection | 10 validation originals | Labels and scores | Checkpoint and threshold |
| Predictive evaluation | 10 test originals: six easy, four medium | Held-out labels | Classification and ranking |
| Guidance qualification | Six medium validation originals | Label-free inference and optimization | Qualify fixed start policy |
| Optimization test | Six distinct medium test originals | Label-free inference and optimization | Frozen-policy comparison |

: Experimental populations and their roles. {#tbl-populations}

Predictive accuracy and optimization utility use distinct populations with fixed parent roles. Optimization-test parents are medium 0, 4, 7, 9, 12 and 20. Parents 9/20 lack admitted predictive-test labels but retain their test role through label-free graphs, without entering fitting or selection.

Guidance validation uses medium 5, 6, 11, 14, 17, and 19. Medium 5 and 6 similarly retain their validation role for label-free optimization despite lacking admitted graph-validation labels. The qualification rule is fixed before validation execution: six valid nonabstained starts, at least four terminal-gap improvements, a nonpositive median guided-minus-control difference, and at most one gap increase exceeding one percentage point. After qualification, the checkpoint, threshold, coverage, and ordering remain fixed for the optimization test.

## Comparisons and time measurements

Each parent uses fresh B/R/G models with identical parameters apart from starting values: one thread, seed 42, a 3,600-second optimization limit and relative tolerance $10^{-4}$. Method order rotates. Incumbents undergo independent feasibility/objective checks.

Root preparation is separate: `Presolve=0`, `NodeLimit=1`, one thread, seed 42 and a 600-second ceiling. During `optimize(callback)`, the first optimal root-node `MIPNODE` event supplies `cbGetNodeRel` values before termination. This is not a separate `model.relax()` solve. The recorded vector enters the graph; a frozen checkpoint in evaluation mode produces scores without gradients. G selects its start, then R matches its counts. Later B/R/G solves reuse these artifacts without rerunning preparation.

Seed 42 fixes a solver search perturbation [@gurobi2026]. `Method=-1` selects the continuous/root algorithm automatically; for MIP roots, the documented usual choice is dual simplex, so this setting alone does not imply non-determinism. Parallel MIP can be deterministic under fixed inputs and environment. Nevertheless, a wall-time limit may stop repeated runs at different work points. We therefore interpret paired outcomes as observations under the stated configuration, without estimating across-seed variability or promising identical terminal states. Comparable settings and stopping rules remain essential [@beiranvand2017].

The primary optimization outcome is the terminal relative MIP gap. It measures the distance between the best feasible objective $z^P$ and the solver's bound $z^D$ on the optimum. For finite nonzero $z^P$, we use $g=|z^P-z^D|/|z^P|$, with explicit handling of unavailable or degenerate values. A smaller gap indicates a tighter optimality certificate. For method $m$, the paired effect is $\Delta g_{pm}=g_{pm}-g_{p,\mathrm{control}}$; multiplying it by 100 gives a percentage-point difference. Negative differences favor guidance. Means, medians, win counts, and leave-out diagnostics summarize these paired observations.

Worker time separates reading/verification, model construction (including LP parsing), optimization, independent audit and residual overhead. Cold application additionally needs feature preparation and inference; artifact reuse still requires verification. Offline training, queueing and orchestration remain separate.

Censoring is defined for each endpoint. A run may attain the 10% gap threshold yet reach the time limit before satisfying the solver’s terminal stopping criterion. An unobserved crossing is censored at the recorded follow-up, not assigned a crossing time of 3,600 seconds. Observed callback times are not exact continuous hitting times, and neither a threshold crossing nor solver-reported optimal status establishes exact mathematical optimality. Parents, not their binary variables, are the solver-comparison units.

## Predictive evaluation metrics {#sec-metrics}

Predictive evaluation measures agreement with checked binary labels, ranking quality, and score reliability. For true positives TP, false positives FP, and false negatives FN, precision is $\mathrm{TP}/(\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FP})$, recall is $\mathrm{TP}/(\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FN})$, and F1 is their harmonic mean. Precision describes the correctness of predicted ones; recall describes how many labelled ones are recovered. Because ones are rare, these measures accompany the receiver operating characteristic area (ROC-AUC), which summarizes discrimination across thresholds [@saito2015].

Average precision (AP) summarizes the precision-recall trade-off as $\mathrm{AP}=\sum_k(R_k-R_{k-1})P_k$, where $P_k$ and $R_k$ are precision and recall at successive distinct score thresholds. Equal scores are evaluated together. This stepwise definition differs from the trapezoidal area under the precision-recall curve (PR-AUC); both quantities are retained separately. The implementation follows the noninterpolated convention described in the scikit-learn metric documentation [@sklearnap].

The Brier score is the mean squared difference between score $q_j$ and label $y_j$, $N^{-1}\sum_j(q_j-y_j)^2$ [@brier1950]. Lower values indicate smaller prediction error. Expected calibration error (ECE) compares predicted positive scores with observed positive frequencies within ten equal-width bins over $[0,1]$:

$$\mathrm{ECE}=\sum_{b=1}^{10}\frac{|S_b|}{N}\left|\overline q_b-\overline y_b\right|.$$

Here, $S_b$ is a score bin; empty bins contribute zero, and score 1 is assigned to the last bin. This binary positive-score diagnostic follows the binned calibration principle discussed by @guo2017, rather than their multiclass top-label confidence definition. Brier and ECE describe score reliability, while BCE describes the training objective. All are reported with their aggregation convention: variable-pooled metrics combine targets across graphs, whereas parent-macro metrics average independently computed parent scores, giving each instance equal weight.

## Reproducibility and data provenance

The [canonical repository](https://github.com/unb-lamfo-or-ai-hpc/cfl-gurobi-gnn) supplies code, splits, protocols, dependencies and rendering instructions; MILPBench supplies original inputs [@milpbench]. SHA256 manifests bind fixed tables and figures, preserving failed attempts separately. Publication builds execute no training, inference or optimization.

Experiments ran on UJA DGX-DaSCI at the Higher Polytechnic School of Jaén, University of Jaén. The supplied DGX-1 inventory lists eight 32-GB Tesla V100 GPUs, two 20-core x86 CPUs at 2.2 GHz, and 512 GB memory. This inventory is not a runtime hardware probe and does not imply allocation of all eight GPUs to training. Historical six-medium workers use one Gurobi thread; the principal CPU comparison uses caps 1/2/4/8/16. Actual allocations and software versions are recorded per run. Storage includes an OS SATA SSD with a 6 Gb/s interface and a four-device SSD RAID-0 array. Interface capacity is distinguished from measured throughput.

Project-owned material uses MIT; benchmark, solver and template retain their rights. Public tables exclude credentials, private paths, raw logs and checkpoints. No unverified Zenodo deposit supports an availability claim.

# Results — historical six-medium study

These archived results are retained with their original populations and budgets.
They are not independent new evidence or the current principal150-row sample.

## Prediction and learning dynamics

The predictive-test graphs contain 5,536,400 binary targets, of which 5,265 take value 1, a prevalence of approximately 0.0951%. @fig-loss shows how training and validation weighted BCE evolve over the 100 epochs and identifies the checkpoint selected by validation.

![Training and validation loss over 100 epochs.](figures/figure_training_validation_loss.pdf){#fig-loss width=95%}

Training BCE falls from 1.5877 to 0.0275; validation BCE reaches its minimum 0.0510 at epoch34 and rises to 0.1124 at epoch100. @tbl-predictive reports the selected checkpoint, not the terminal state.

{{< include tables/current_predictive.qmd >}}

Precision/recall are 0.6923/0.7064, pooled F1 is 0.6993 and parent-macro F1 is 0.7027. AP0.7745 and trapezoidal PR-AUC0.7747 remain distinct. ROC-AUC, Brier and ECE complement prediction, not solver-performance evidence.

## Guidance validation

The six-instance validation comparison satisfies the precommitted qualification rule. Solver messages confirm that all learned starts are loaded, with no policy abstention. Four reduce terminal gap; the median difference is -1.224 percentage points, and one increase exceeds one percentage point. Medium 19 reports zero terminal gap after approximately 671 seconds, while its unguided control reaches the time limit. The validation observations are displayed alongside the distinct test observations in @fig-effects below; only the validation observations qualify the policy.

@tbl-heldout compares terminal gaps and first observed 10% crossings for all six optimization-test instances. Each row pairs the unguided and learned-start runs of the same mathematical model. A negative gap difference favors the learned start; a censored crossing indicates that the 10% target was not observed within the budget.

{{< include tables/current_heldout.qmd >}}

Historically, learned starts reduce terminal gap on five of six instances, median difference -1.164 percentage points. Medium12/20 dominate the decreases. Medium0 reaches10% earlier despite a worse terminal gap; medium4 shows the reverse. @fig-effects separates validation from optimization-test differences.

![Paired terminal-gap differences by instance.](figures/figure_validation_test_gap_effects.pdf){#fig-effects width=95%}

## Influence and computational cost

To assess how individual instances affect the aggregate result, @tbl-influence reports the complete six-instance summary and two leave-out diagnostics. The diagnostics retain the original fixed policy and do not redefine the test population.

{{< include tables/current_influence.qmd >}}

The mean paired difference is -7.200 percentage points across all six instances. It is -1.659 points without medium 20 and -0.556 points without medium 12 and 20; the corresponding medians are -1.164, -0.213, and -0.140 points. The favorable direction persists in these diagnostics, while the magnitude changes appreciably. The matched root-LP comparator improves terminal gap on one of six test instances, with a median difference of approximately +1.124 points relative to control. @tbl-times complements the gap results with optimization and worker elapsed times.

{{< include tables/current_timing.qmd >}}

Medium12/20 use approximately702/1,585solver seconds with GNN. Four GNN runs and all comparator runs reach the time limit before attaining the solver’s terminal criterion. This does not mean their 10% crossing is necessarily censored: medium0/4 attain that threshold with GNN before termination. Worker time includes verification, model construction and auditing, but excludes feature preparation/inference; it is not complete cold application time.

# Discussion

Historical gap improvements illustrate the potential of partial starts, while the principal retrospective comparison shows how effects depend on the parent, thread cap and cost boundary. A smaller terminal gap may reflect primal improvement, a stronger dual bound, or both. It does not by itself measure acceleration, and a solver-only gain can disappear once preparation costs are included.

The interface preserves the original feasible region: unlike learned restrictions [@qu2026], supplied Start values guide an attempt that Gurobi may complete, repair or reject. This connects learned information to a conventional solver [@bengio2021]. However, the matched R/G comparison does not isolate the effect of ones-first ordering. It matches support and positive counts, while R depends on G's preparation. The observed differences concern the complete supplied starts, not a causal advantage of the selector alone.

The same distinction applies to repeatability. Automatic root-method selection does not invalidate an observed comparison, but identical parameter settings do not establish a distribution of expected performance. One solver seed per principal configuration leaves search-path variability unquantified. We report the observed outcomes and their numerical and censoring restrictions, rather than treating thread caps or repeated measurements as independent problem instances. Rare-positive prediction metrics [@saito2015] and calibration diagnostics [@brier1950; @guo2017] answer different questions from solver utility.

The GPU comparison reinforces this separation: training accelerates, but selected F1 declines and assigned GPU-hours increase. It does not show that faster training preserves prediction quality or improves the resulting starts. The longer-horizon CPU campaign remains in progress and supplies no final efficacy conclusion at this stage.

# Final considerations, limitations and future work

The study provides an auditable partial-start pipeline and a scoped computational assessment. Historical six-medium improvements and the principal analysis of 150 seed-42 rows describe different populations. Neither establishes universal GNN superiority, population-level significance, exact optimality or independent generalization.

Labels are checked feasible incumbents, but may be approximate, and quality screening selects a tractable subset. Agreement with one such label is not optimization quality. Historically exposed test parents, absent hard-instance results and numerical sensitivity further restrict the conclusions. Adverse pilot outcomes remain part of the evidence; changes in training population prevent a causal attribution to the selector.

Sensitivity to solver seeds, explicit root algorithms and neural hyperparameters remains unresolved. A proportionate extension would vary one factor at a time: first solver seeds with frozen starts, then a root-method comparison if logs identify a relevant uncertainty, and targeted depth/width or training-seed checks if required by a stronger predictive claim. Such studies would retain validation-only selection, matched controls, censoring and preparation costs. They are future work, not completed evidence. Deferring them requires limiting the present claims; a limitations statement cannot establish robustness that was not tested.

The original CPU checkpoint is retained while the approved four-medium campaign awaits its final return and metric-specific review. The completed serial/DDP pair contributes a negative quality finding. Additional independent instances and mechanism ablations could strengthen interpretation. Augmentation and network-science visualizations are not completed contributions. The curated archive must preserve unsuccessful attempts and undergo redistribution-rights and deposit verification; no Zenodo DOI is claimed as reserved or published.
